Commensal

/kuh-MEN-sul/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Commensal means relating to a biological relationship in which one organism benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed.

Commensal means relating to a biological relationship in which one organism benefits while the other is neither helped nor harmed. Cattle egrets have a commensal relationship with grazing buffalo: the birds feast on insects the herd stirs up, and the buffalo gain nothing and lose nothing.

Worked Example

A remora fastens itself to the underside of a shark with a suction disc on top of its head. It rides along for weeks, snapping up scraps that drift loose whenever the shark feeds. The shark's swimming, hunting, and health are unchanged; it appears not to register the passenger at all. Biologists call this arrangement commensal because exactly one animal profits and the other simply carries on.

One organism (the remora) gains food while the other (the shark) is neither helped nor harmed, which is precisely what commensal describes.

How Commensal Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

coexisting

coexisting: living alongside another species without conflict

cohabiting

cohabiting: sharing the same living space with another organism

Antonyms

mutualistic

mutualistic: describing a relationship in which both organisms benefit

parasitic

parasitic: describing a relationship in which one organism benefits by harming its host

How Strong Is It? — neutral → exploitative → commensal

neutral vs. commensal

neutral vs. commensal: A neutral relationship leaves both species exactly as they were, while a commensal one gives a clear advantage to one of them.

exploitative vs. commensal

exploitative vs. commensal: A commensal partner takes its benefit without costing the other anything, but an exploitative one takes that benefit directly at the other's expense.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of commensal.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — com

Prefix — com: together, with

Root — mens

Root — mens: from Latin mensa, table

Suffix — al

Suffix — al: characteristic of, pertaining to, having the nature of

Put it together

Put it together: Commensal is built from com- ('together, with'), the Latin root mensa ('table'), and the suffix -al ('characteristic of, pertaining to'). Read the pieces in order and the word means 'characteristic of sharing a table': one guest eats at the table, and the host is no worse off for it.

Use the root in a new word: mesa

Use the root in a new word: mesa: A mesa rises from the desert with a top as flat and level as a table, which is exactly what its Latin ancestor mensa means.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal, scientific (biology) register

Commensal almost always modifies a relationship, a species, or an organism, as in 'a commensal relationship' or 'commensal bacteria.' Save it for cases where exactly one partner gains and the other is genuinely unaffected; if both partners gain, the word you want is mutualistic.
